The Later 1970s: Gas Lines, Starfields, and the End of One American Mood

A decade caught between a shark fin and a starship, a gas pump and a golden record sailing into the dark.

↓ SCROLL TO BEGIN ↓
PART 01 Saigon · Watergate · Bicentennial

Looking Backward

By the middle of the 1970s, the United States was tired in a way that went deeper than politics. The Vietnam War had cracked public trust. Watergate had broken faith in the presidency. Inflation made everyday life more expensive. Gasoline shortages made people wait in long lines. The country still had power, wealth, and imagination, but its confidence had been dented.

Then came April 30, 1975. Saigon, the capital of South Vietnam, fell to North Vietnamese forces. Helicopters lifted Americans and some South Vietnamese allies from rooftops and evacuation points as the war reached its final chapter. The United States had already withdrawn its combat troops after the 1973 Paris Peace Accords, but the fall of Saigon marked the collapse of South Vietnam and the end of the long war America had fought to prevent that outcome.

For many Americans, it felt like defeat, even if leaders used more careful language. The war did not end with a parade. It ended with evacuation, exhaustion, and unanswered questions.

In 1976, America celebrated its Bicentennial, two hundred years since the Declaration of Independence in 1776. There were fireworks, tall ships, parades, commemorative coins, patriotic television specials, and red-white-and-blue everything. The federal government had created an American Revolution Bicentennial Administration to coordinate national commemorations.

But the Bicentennial was not simple self-congratulation. It happened after Vietnam and Watergate, when Americans were asking whether the country had lived up to its founding promises. The celebration had two faces: one looking proudly at 1776, the other looking nervously at 1976. It was a birthday party held in a house where the adults had been arguing all night.

That tension is the key to the later 1970s: the United States kept producing symbols of hope, invention, and spectacle, but underneath them ran a low electric hum of doubt.

★ Pause and Reflect ★

The Two-Faced Birthday Party

The Bicentennial is described as a celebration with "two faces." One face looked at 1776 with pride. The other face looked at 1976 with worry.

Think for a moment before scrolling on:

  • Why might a country want to throw a huge birthday party precisely when it is feeling its worst?
  • Have you ever seen a celebration that felt like it was trying too hard? What did that look like?
  • What does it mean for a society to "look up to its founding promises"? Whose promises were they originally?

Hold this image in your head: a birthday party held in a house where the adults have been arguing all night. It will help every section that follows.

PART 02 Pumps Closed · Politics of Scarcity

The Empty Tank

For much of the postwar era, Americans had lived as if energy would stay cheap forever. Cars grew large. Suburbs spread outward. Highways stitched the country together. Air conditioning, appliances, plastics, and mass production all depended on oil, electricity, and fuel.

The 1970s interrupted that assumption.

The first major shock came after the 1973 Arab oil embargo, when oil-producing countries restricted exports in response to U.S. support for Israel during the Yom Kippur War. The U.S. State Department describes the embargo as a major strain on an American economy increasingly dependent on foreign oil. The Department of Energy's timeline notes that the embargo began October 17, 1973, and helped spark the first "energy crisis."

The problem did not vanish in the later 1970s. Energy insecurity returned with force during the 1979 Iranian Revolution, when oil supplies were disrupted and prices rose again. Ordinary people experienced the crisis not as theory, but as frustration: gas lines, higher prices, smaller cars, thermostat rules, and a sense that the mighty American machine could suddenly sputter.

This mattered politically. Jimmy Carter, elected president in 1976 and inaugurated in January 1977, treated energy as a serious national problem. He spoke about conservation, sacrifice, and long-term planning. That was realistic, but it was not always popular. Americans did not necessarily want a president who told them the age of easy abundance might be ending. Carter's honesty could sound like weakness to people who wanted reassurance.

"The 1960s asked, 'Can America become more just?'
The 1970s added another question:
'Can America keep living the way it has been living?'"
◇ Recall Practice ◇

Test yourself without scrolling back up

  • What event in 1973 triggered the first major U.S. energy crisis?
  • Why did Carter's honesty about energy "sound like weakness" to some Americans?
  • Which 1979 event caused the second big shock to American oil supplies?

1. The Arab oil embargo, which began October 17, 1973, in response to U.S. support of Israel during the Yom Kippur War.

2. Americans wanted reassurance and easy abundance. A president speaking about sacrifice, smaller cars, and limits felt like a downgrade in the national mood.

3. The Iranian Revolution disrupted oil supplies again in 1979, leading to a second round of gas lines and price spikes.

PART 03 Garages · Sharks · Sketch Comedy

Imagination Did Not Quit

While trust in government weakened, culture exploded in strange, brilliant directions.

In 1975, Microsoft was founded by Bill Gates and Paul Allen in Albuquerque, New Mexico. At the time, personal computing was still a small world of hobbyists, kits, and early machines. Microsoft's early work focused on software, including BASIC for microcomputers. It did not yet look like an empire. It looked like a few young people staring at the edge of a new machine age.

That same year, Jaws opened and changed Hollywood. Steven Spielberg's shark thriller was marketed as a national event and became one of the biggest moneymakers in film history up to that point. The Library of Congress notes that its television-heavy marketing campaign and enormous box office helped create the model of the modern summer blockbuster. The monster in the water was fictional, but the business lesson was real: movies could arrive like invasions.

Also in 1975, Saturday Night Live began on NBC. Its first episode aired October 11, 1975, hosted by George Carlin. The show brought a looser, stranger, more irreverent kind of comedy to late-night television. It felt like television had discovered sarcasm and invited it to stay.

In 1976, Apple Computer was founded by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. The Library of Congress describes Apple's founding as tied to a vision of changing how people viewed computers. Like Microsoft, Apple began small, but it pointed toward a future where computers would not belong only to governments, universities, and corporations.

Then, in 1977, Star Wars opened. It mixed myth, science fiction, old adventure serials, samurai echoes, desert loneliness, rebellion, empire, and glowing swords. It was not just a film. It became a shared modern legend. The Library of Congress later recognized Star Wars as part of America's film heritage through the National Film Registry.

The country had lost faith in many leaders, but it had not lost its ability to imagine.

★ Pause and Reflect ★

Why does culture explode when politics collapses?

Look at the years 1975 to 1977. Microsoft. Apple. Jaws. Saturday Night Live. Star Wars. All in roughly a 24-month window. All while the country was, by most reports, demoralized.

  • Why might trust in institutions fall just as creative output rises?
  • Which of these inventions or works do you think changed daily life the most? Which had the deepest cultural impact? Are those the same answer?
  • If you had been a young adult in 1975 with a garage and an idea, what would you have built?
PART 04 Voyager · Disco · Punk Rock

Two Soundtracks, One Decade

In 1977, NASA launched Voyager 2 on August 20 and Voyager 1 on September 5. Their mission was to explore the outer planets, but they eventually traveled far beyond their original plans. NASA notes that both spacecraft became the only probes to operate outside the Sun's heliosphere, the protective bubble created by solar particles and magnetic fields.

Each Voyager carried a Golden Record, a kind of message-in-a-bottle for the cosmos: sounds, music, greetings, and images meant to represent Earth. That is one of the most haunting facts of the decade. While people on Earth argued over gas, war, inflation, and politics, two little machines carried human music into deep space.

Back home, music split into bright mirrors and broken glass.

Disco rose out of dance clubs, especially from Black, Latino, and gay communities, before becoming a national craze. The Smithsonian notes that disco was rooted in nonwhite and gay communities and that Saturday Night Fever helped mark the peak of the craze. Disco was rhythm, lights, release, bodies moving after years of bad news. It was not merely shiny clothes and dance floors. It was also urban nightlife, community, sexuality, escape, and style.

But across town, sometimes literally, punk rock kicked the door in. Punk was fast, raw, sarcastic, and often angry. Britannica describes punk as an aggressive rock movement that coalesced internationally from about 1975 to 1980. The Ramones in New York made songs short, loud, and stripped down. The Sex Pistols in Britain turned outrage into spectacle. Britannica identifies them as central to the British punk movement of the late 1970s. The Clash added sharper politics, reggae influence, and working-class fury.

Disco said, "Dance while the city burns."
Punk said, "Name the fire."
◇ Recall and Connect ◇

The decade's two soundtracks

Without scrolling back, try to fill in these blanks in your head:

  • Voyager 1 launched in September 1977. What did each Voyager carry that was meant for non-human listeners?
  • Disco grew out of which three communities, according to the Smithsonian?
  • Name one famous American punk band and one famous British punk band from this period.
  • How would you describe the difference in attitude between disco and punk in one sentence?

1. The Golden Record, with sounds, music, greetings, and images representing Earth.

2. Black, Latino, and gay communities.

3. American: the Ramones. British: the Sex Pistols, or the Clash.

4. Disco offered release and escape from bad news. Punk named the bad news directly and shouted at it. One soundtrack covered the fire. The other pointed at the fire.

PART 05 Carter · Tehran · The Doorway

444 Days

Jimmy Carter entered the White House after Watergate promising honesty, humility, and moral seriousness. He was a former Georgia governor, a Navy veteran, a peanut farmer, and a born-again Christian. Gerald Ford's presidential library notes that Carter narrowly defeated Ford in the 1976 election to become the 39th president.

Carter had real achievements, including the 1978 Camp David Accords between Egypt and Israel, but his presidency became increasingly associated with inflation, energy problems, and a feeling of national drift. Then came the crisis that damaged him most.

On November 4, 1979, Iranian students seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and took Americans hostage. The crisis lasted 444 days, ending on January 20, 1981, the day Ronald Reagan was inaugurated. The National Archives describes it as a major international crisis caused by the seizure of the embassy and its employees by revolutionary Iranian students backed by Iran's Ayatollah Khomeini-led government. White House Historical Association materials note that 66 American diplomats and military personnel were initially taken hostage.

The crisis badly damaged Carter's reputation because it made the United States look powerless on television night after night. Americans saw blindfolded hostages, angry crowds, and a president unable to bring citizens home quickly. This does not mean Carter did nothing. Diplomacy, sanctions, negotiations, and a failed rescue mission were all part of the story. But politics is partly perception, and the perception was devastating.

So the later 1970s ended with a country caught between two futures. One future was digital, cinematic, cosmic: Microsoft, Apple, Star Wars, Voyager. The other was anxious and unstable: oil shocks, inflation, hostage tapes, and distrust. The decade that began with Watergate's wreckage closed with embassy gates locked in Tehran.

And somewhere in the static between disco basslines and punk guitars, between a shark fin and a starship, between a gas pump and a golden record sailing into the dark, the 1980s were waiting.

Part V. Extended Response

Essay · No Auto Grading · Save Your Answer Locally
The reading describes the later 1970s as a decade caught between "a digital, cinematic, cosmic" future and "an anxious and unstable" one. In a focused essay of roughly 400 to 600 words, choose a position on the following question and defend it with at least three specific examples from the reading:

Did the later 1970s feel more like an ending or more like a beginning? Why?
Suggestions before you write:
  • Open with a clear thesis sentence that answers the question directly.
  • Use at least three concrete details from the reading. Possible material: Saigon, Watergate, the Bicentennial, the energy crises, Microsoft and Apple, Jaws and Star Wars, Voyager, disco and punk, Carter, the Iran hostage crisis.
  • Anticipate the other side of the argument. The strongest essays acknowledge the counter-case before refuting it.
  • Close with one sentence that returns to your thesis but adds a fresh observation, not a repeat.
